subsubtopic: JURISDICTION OVER CANADIAN WATERS-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43 on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity. In view of the controversy which exists between France and Canada over the ownership of fishing and mineral rights on Canada's continental shelf between mainland France and the offshore islands of St. Pierre and Miquelon which are now classed as French provinces, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Malpeque (Mr. Gass):
That the Canadian government communicate with the French government, emphatically informing that government that the so-called disputed waters, which cover part of the Hibernia and Ben Nevis oil Fields, are sovereign Canadian waters and resources.

subsubtopic: OIL INDUSTRY CONTRIBUTIONS TO POLITICAL PARTIES- MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43 on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity. In view of the fact that both the Liberal and Conservative parties buried the oil industry price Fixing report for the past eight years, and that the protection money in the form of political contributions paid by the oil majors totalled close to half a million dollars between 1974 and 1977, over $190,000 to the Liberal Party and over $250,000 to the Tory party, rising to $192,504 to the Liberals in 1978 alone, with pay-offs increasing in recent years, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Broadview-Greenwood (Mr. Rae):
That this House can only draw one conclusion from the fact that the major oil companies have contributed over half a million dollars since 1974 to the Liberals and Conservatives; that the oil industry price fixing report was buried for eight years and was finally brought to light on Wednesday, March 4, 1981, and the conclusion is that while these political donations were initially sufficient to provide the necessary protection, clearly they did not keep up with inflation and the Liberal Party's rising business costs-in particular hyper inflation in the pork market-and expresses its regret at the embarrassment thus caused to the oil majors and their insurance agents, the Liberal and Conservative parties of Canada.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43. A
Section 47 investigation under the Combines Investigation Act
is currently being conducted into the relationship between Bell Canada and Northern Telecom. The Restrictive Trade Practices Commission held almost four years of hearings, sat 224 days, travelled the entire country, heard 230 witnesses to date, generated 34,000 pages of evidence, and received some 2,000 exhibits. Despite the fact the hearings are vitally important to telephone subscribers and the Canadian electronics industry, there has been no visible public debate; indeed, very few Canadians are even aware of the inquiry.
In light of the statement of the director, Mr. Bertrand, that a Section 47 inquiry on price-fixing in the oil industry "will have a significant role in placing the importance of competition in the petroleum industry in the forefront of public debate", with which proposition the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Ouellet) wholly concurs, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Saskatoon West (Mr. Hnatyshyn):
That this House directs the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs to make a statement on motions on the reasons for referring the director's report on oil industry price-fixing to the Restrictive Trade Practices Commission, which presumably has the function to make representations to change Canada's competition law, thereby delaying action for a number of years by the commission which exercises powers of holding hearings in secret.

speechtext: Madam Speaker, not surprisingly I have a series of questions this morning for the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources. Madam Speaker, I should like to take advantage of Standing Order 68(2) to give a succinct explanation of the provisions of this bill.
The purpose of this bill is to define the exception in the present law that allows an abortion where there is "danger to the health" of a pregnant woman should the pregnancy continue.
The bill is consistent with the intent of the present law as expressed by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Chretien) when he introduced it in 1969. He left no doubt that the original intention of the legislation was that "therapeutic abortions" would be an exceptional procedure, invoked only after strict compliance with the law: the abortion was to be performed by a medical practitioner supported by a therapeutic abortion committee of medical practitioners in an approved hospital, and it was to be performed only where the health or life of the mother is in danger.

speechtext:
1.	Has the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs pursued the complaint under Section 7 of the Combines Investigation Act concerning the mini-land bridge rate in Vancouver and, if not, is it because of the difficulty in obtaining a conviction?

speakeroldname: Mr. D. M. Collenette (Parliamentary Secretary to President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
subsubtopic: MINI-LAND BRIDGE RATES, VANCOUVER
speechtext:
I am informed by the Departments of Consumer and Corporate Affairs and Transport as follows:
I.	Upon receipt of the six-resident application under Section 7 of the Combines Investigation Act for an inquiry into miniland bridge rates, the Director of Investigation and Research immediately commenced an inquiry into the matter. The director has very recently concluded that the matter being inquired into does not justify further inquiry and. pursuant toSection 14 of the Combines Investigation Act, advised the minister and the applicant of such a fact.
2.	The policy regarding licensing of transportation firms in Canada is contained in the various acts governing modes of transportation under federal jurisdiction: the Railway Act, the Aeronautics Act, the Transport Act (for marine) and the National Transportation Act (for solids pipelines). The general test that is employed to determine whether or not a licence should be issued is whether a proposed service is and will be required by the present and future public convenience and necessity. No specific directions "to ensure fair competition" or "to safeguard Canadian interests" are included in legislation. However, the general nature of the public convenience and necessity test allows the Canadian Transport Commission to consider a wide variety of factors which it, the applicant or any intervenor may wish to bring to bear in connection with an application for a licence. National transportation policy (as enunciated in Section 3 of the National Transportation Act) calls for "an economic, efficient and adequate transportation system making the best use of all available modes of transportation at the lowest total cost." This general policy applies to modes of transport under federal jurisdiction.

speechtext:

3.	What are the options being considered by the government as indicated by the deputy minister of communications?

speakeroldname: Mr. Peter Stollery (Parliamentary Secretary to Secretary of State and Minister of Communications):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Communications; Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State of Canada
subsubtopic: CANADA-U.S. SATELLITE COMPETITION
speechtext:
In so far as the
Department of Communications is concerned, the reply to the above question is as follows: 1. Yes. Should the use of domestic satellite facilities for transborder telephone, data and video traffic be approved, the government is concerned that an imbalance favouring the use of U.S. satellites might develop if firms headquartered in the U.S., which would use U.S. systems for their U.S. domestic requirements, were to make use of these systems to serve their Canadian offices as well. This could adversely affect existing arrangements between the domestic common carriers on both sides of the border which ensure the equitable sharing of terrestrial traffic and revenues, as well as the provision of some Canadian traffic carried on Canadian facilities. Until the kinds of systems and services which eventually might be established are known with greater certainty, it would not be possible to develop accurate projections of the likely impact on existing systems.

Both sides recognize the need to meet our international obligations under the Intelsat Agreement and to proceed carefully in introducing any transborder satellite services; further discussions will take place at an appropriate time. At present an exchange of letters in 1972 permits such services to be established only under very limited circumstances.

speechtext:
that Bill C-55, an act to amend the Canada Student Loans Act, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Communications and Culture.
He said: First of all, Madam Speaker, I would like to begin my comments on this bill which is rather important for Canadian students by thanking the members of the opposition. I had discussions first of all with the hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Nielsen), then with the hon. member for Mission-Port Moody (Mr. Rose), after which my own House leader met with the other House leaders who agreed that this bill could go through all stages today, and those who will benefit most from this will be the students of this country.

Bill C-55 proposes amendments to the Canada Student Loans Act. This act, which is well-known to hon. members, enables full-time post-secondary students in financial need to obtain loans to assist them in meeting their educational costs, where they would be otherwise unable to pursue their personal educational goals.
The amount of loan assistance granted to any individual is determined by provincial authorities in accordance with minimum criteria agreed to by all participating provincial govern-
March 6, 1981

merits and, of course, the federal government. The loans are advanced by chartered banks or other designated lenders such as credit unions. The Canadian government pays the interest charges on the loans while the students are enrolled in universities or community colleges and for a six-month period thereafter and guarantees lenders against any loss under the program.
The act was introduced in 1964 and has been amended only once, in 1970, although changes in loan limits have been effected twice by means of appropriations items, the most recent in 1975.
[ Translation]
I could perhaps add at this time, Madam Speaker, that this program of course applies throughout Canada, but that the province of Quebec has opted out, which means that while this legislation does not apply to individual students in Quebec, the amounts will be transferred to the Quebec government to finance student assistance programs. This year, nearly $21 million will be transferred to the Quebec government under this program, and since this program was implemented in 1964, over $126 million have been transferred to the Quebec government to be made available to Canadian students who are residents of Quebec.

I should like to emphasize how much I appreciate the co-operation of all parties in the House which has allowed this bill to be brought forward for second reading at this time. Even though we are all preoccupied with the overwhelmingly important issue of constitutional reform, this bill is an essential piece of business since it will afford many young Canadians, approximately 6,000 per year, across Canada access to student loans to continue their education. In many cases they would otherwise be unable to do so.
One of the most important amendments proposed in this bill arises from the need to accommodate the increase in the number of courses less than the traditional 26 weeks in length which are available to young people as a result of the rapid growth in the number of community colleges and technical and vocational institutes at the post-secondary level. The main effect of this bill is to make students in community colleges qualify for aid under the Canada Student Loans Act.
At the other end of the spectrum the bill also provides for increased loans to students enrolled in courses longer than the traditional university academic year of 32 weeks, thus making it more practical for such students to continue their education without undue financial hardship.
The current legislation provides for a maximum loan of $1,800 in an academic year of at least 26 weeks' duration, as hon. members know. The bill before us proposes instead that loans be available to persons in periods of study of at least 12 weeks' duration. This amendment takes into consideration changes which have occurred in Canadian educational patterns since the initial bill was introduced.
Student Loans
The bill also proposes that the loan limit of $1,800 be expressed on a weekly basis, thus relating the maximum amount of loan aid a student may receive to the length of his or her course and, therefore, to the costs. The proposed weekly loan limit of $56.25 amounts to $1,800 for a 32-week course, the traditional university course length in which the majority of students are enrolled. Since the current legislation entitles students in 26 to 31-week courses and in semesters of 13 to 15 weeks, which form part of a longer course, to $1,800 and $900 respectively, we are providing in the bill that such students remain eligible for loans up to these limits rather than the lesser amounts which would result if the $56.25 weekly limit were to be applied. This is particularly important in certain cases, notably that of students at Memorial University in Newfoundland.
These two proposals will go some way toward meeting the financial needs of both those enrolled in colleges of applied arts and technology and similar institutions in courses between 12 and 26 weeks in length and those enrolled in courses longer than 32 weeks.
I might mention here that some provinces have suggested that the maximum loan limits should be raised substantially to provide more aid to needy students. However, at the same time, student groups generally have indicated strong opposition to any substantial increase in loan limits, insisting that loans should be replaced by non-repayable grants.
Of course, members of the House will be aware that a federal-provincial task force on student assistance was set up early in 1980 to examine the whole question of student assistance in Canada. The report of that task force was received by the Council of Ministers of Education and by myself at a meeting in Fredericton, New Brunswick, on January 27, 1981. The report includes a review of past studies in the area of student assistance, both in Canada and elsewhere. It also includes an analysis of existing student aid programs in Canada, the potential future trends which might bear on student aid in the 1980s, the principles and objectives which should govern student aid, and five program alternatives compatible with those principles and objectives.
The task force does not make specific recommendations, since it is intended to prompt public reaction. The Council and I, when releasing the report, invited comments on it from student groups, other interested groups and the general public by June 1 of this year. This input is expected to be considered by the Council of Ministers of Education and by myself in the fall with a view to considering what changes, if any, may be required in provincial and federal student assistance programs in Canada.
This bill, therefore, while important, does not propose sweeping changes to the program at the moment, but changes that we believe are essential to update the act in light of changing course patterns. Thus, it will not pre-empt any decisions which may flow from the work of the task force.
In addition to the important modification I have mentioned already, the bill proposes several amendments of a housekeeping nature. First, it proposes dropping the current requirement
7988

March 6, 1981

for a 12-month waiting period before applications may be accepted from those with permanent resident status. As members know, the Immigration Act of 1977 no longer permits a student to convert student visa status to permanent resident status while in Canada. Hence, the need for the waiting period is no longer relevant and it has been removed. I am sure this is a modification which will be welcomed by many students in this country who are here from other countries.
The bill also proposes inclusion of specific authority for the governor in council to make regulations respecting the denial of further assistance to those deliberately abusing the program. It also includes authorization for the governor in council to make regulations restricting payments to banks under the guarantee where a bank has failed, without cause, to submit claims for loss promptly, thus avoiding unnecessary accumulation of interest charges against the student borrower. The bill also provides for a change in the minister responsible, consequent upon the transfer of the program from the Department of Finance to the Department of the Secretary of State.
Finally, the bill includes the alteration of the loan year start date from July 1 to August 1 to coincide with the banking fiscal year, thereby facilitating interest payments to lenders.
In closing, I would like to emphasize that the amendments proposed are in some regards very important, particularly as they concern community college students and people in Canada who are here on a permanent resident basis. Many of the amendments are of a housekeeping nature, which are needed to update the legislation and are, of course, important in that respect to many students. I had occasion last spring to review with the National Union of Students the need for such changes as we are now proposing in this bill.
As I have also mentioned, the task force on student assistance has completed its report and interested groups are invited to comment upon it. When that process is complete, consideration will be given to the future direction of student assistance programs at both the provincial and federal levels of government. While some provincial authorities would prefer to see loan limits raised and while student groups oppose such a move, I believe both groups support the technical amendments proposed as a short-term measure.
Hon. members will appreciate that should this bill be acceded to it will be necessary to print and issue with dispatch new brochures to all concerned, together with the necessary modified application forms. The lead time for such printing will be some two months. And if the measures are to take effect for the 1981-82 school year, and I know all members are interested in seeing that it does come into effect as soon as possible, the necessary materials will have to be in the hands of students prior to the end of the current academic year in the spring of 1981. That is the main reason why I have asked members on all sides of the House for their co-operation in seeing that this bill be adopted as soon as possible.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 rise to participate in this debate on Bill C-55, to amend the Canada Student Loans Act. I can assure the Secretary of
State (Mr. Fox) who so ably discussed the bill on second reading, that he does have our co-operation. But there are a few points that 1 would like to raise at this time. We understand the urgency to have this bill go through all readings today because of the 1981-1982 student year. No doubt these amendments are long overdue. In fact, some of them may not go far enough. However, we must deal with the bill as it is, and we propose to do so.
There are a few points I would like to make concerning student aid. When the program was set up in 1964, the principle of it was to help needy students obtain a post-secondary education. To a great extent I think this program has been successful and it has achieved that objective. As with most government programs, there are cases of abuse. I think that many of these cases could be eliminated if the income verification rate had to be, by law, higher than the present 5 per cent. I know that some provinces have a 100 per cent verification requirement applicable to parents' income and assets before consideration is given to loan applications. But that is not the case in all provinces. I think it is one area that we could possibly look at.
In view of the rumoured and much discussed possibility of the federal government's threatened cutbacks or elimination of federal funding to universities to the tune of approximately $1.5 billion, which has not as yet been denied by the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) or the minister responsible for social development, I am sure that this act is only temporary. In fact, if that aid does not go to the provinces for post-secondary education, the burden of financing those programs will drop back on to the students and their parents, the provincial governments, or a combination of both. I imagine that we may be taking a long, hard look at this bill next year if that funding is changed with respect to the provincial governments. The fiscal agreement expires in March of 1982, which does not leave the government too much time to come up with a policy which will aid students if those cutbacks are carried out. If the cutbacks are carried out, I am sure we will be looking at a maximum loan of $9,800 in a lifetime. That figure would have to be reviewed, and reviewed rather quickly.
I am happy to see that the amendments will provide authority to relate the maximum repayment period to the size of the debt within the statutory maximum repayment period of ten years. It has been a little unrealistic to allow a student who may have borrowed $500 or $1,000 ten years to repay that loan. I am glad that has been amended within the act, because it has been an unnecessary expense to the government. I am also pleased to see the provisions to exclude students who default without just cause from further benefits, and I think that is a very important amendment.
A couple of areas that I would like to discuss may cause some controversy, but I think I would be negating my responsibility if I did not touch on them. The assessment process should, in my opinion, be universal. All provinces should adhere to the same criteria. Income and assets should be taken

into consideration, and I alluded to that earlier. This would probably eliminate some of the abuse of the program, although I must say I am very pleased to note that abuse of the program is not high. However, as a Member of Parliament 1 have, as 1 am sure most hon. members in the House have, had constituents tell me that there are some students getting loans within a community whose parents could well afford to help them out with their education. The fact that students are left with a deficit between need and aid reflects the necessity of reviewing the loan limits.
Another concern I have is the loans for offshore education. In 1978 and 1979, the figure reached approximately $4.25 million, primarily going into the United States, with $500,000 for the United Kingdom; $343,000 for Europe and about $150,000 for the rest of the world.
My concern is not the amount of money which is being loaned, but the monitoring of the standards of education from these offshore institutions. It is safe to say, I think, that most of the institutions have standards which compare favourably to Canadian institutions. However, a small percentage do not meet Canadian standards. The provinces, which submit the list of approved institutions to the student loans program, may have difficulty in monitoring standards and ensuring that students educated at offshore institutions will meet and match the requirements of the particular faculty of study in Canada. I think specifically of the medical profession, where students may study medicine at a university or medical school offshore, having used a loan from the program, only to find that they cannot pass the medical boards when they come back to Canada. This type of occurrence should be carefully looked at, either by the provinces under whose jurisdiction this falls, or if necessary, to save frustration and expense, by the federal program, which may have better or more able resources available through their consulates.
The eligible course length change is a long overdue measure. However, even the provision to include 12 week-courses is not, in my opinion, enough. This allows many community college and technical courses to be included, but it does not include apprenticeship programs.
I would like to talk for just a moment about recognized apprenticeship programs where there is block institutional training. In other words, an apprentice will work for a period of ten months, on-the-job training, and then will go to an institution for block training program. For those eight weeks, the student must apply for unemployment insurance. The first lesson we teach a young apprentice is how to apply for unemployment insurance. I think that is very regrettable, and I would ask the minister, in the review of the program, now that loan capabilities have been reduced on a weekly basis, which I think is excellent, to take a look at the apprenticeship program. I would much rather teach an apprentice how to borrow student funding and pay it back to the government than how to apply for unemployment insurance while he is continuing his education. An apprenticeship program is post-secondary education. It is just as important to this country as a university education or a community college education. Apprenticeship

programs are very important in this country today, particularly with the critical skills shortage we have here. Some of the apprenticeship institutional training is done four days on the job and one day in the school. That is a little easier. This task force was put together by the Clark government, and I was pleased to read what is a very good report. He said: Mr. Speaker, there is no need for me to speak at length this afternoon because, by its very nature, this piece of legislation should not be the subject of a protracted debate since, in that respect, it is our constitutional obligation here in the House-it is the only group of individuals, excepting hon. members of course, whose salaries are set by the House of Commons under the Constitution.
We already had a debate on second reading. We also had debates in committee and the bill is now back before the House with a few amendments because, in light of discussions in committee, the controversial aspect of the contributions of judges to their pension plan had to be reviewed. On behalf of the government, I committed myself before the members of the committee to appoint a review committee to re-examine the entire question of the pension of judges and the contribution they should make.

The judges have not had a salary increase for some time. The last one, in 1975, totalled 7.5 per cent. Therefore, this measure is long overdue. The members of the committee agreed that it is very important, if we are to attract good judges, that they should be able to do their job without any financial preoccupation. The committee recognized that the level of compensation for judges, compared to what used to be the level in relation to public servants and professionals, indicates they have lost a lot of ground since 1976. Therefore, this bill is long overdue.
The history of this bill is that the Dorfman committee studied this problem as well as a committee of the Canadian Bar Association, presided over by a member of the Quebec bar. A year ago last December my predecessor, Senator Flynn, made a commitment to proceed quickly, but it took some time before we could proceed. In any event, I think we now have a bill which is acceptable, and I recommend its adoption in this House.
I do not intend to elaborate; the bill speaks for itself. It is very important that we pass it and that the judges be accorded what they deserve for the good job all of them do for Canada. We are all proud of our judiciary. It is efficient, competent and completely independent from the executive and legislative bodies. I hope this bill will tell them that the Canadian people appreciate the work they are doing to maintain justice in our society.

I accept the admonition of the minister that he has accepted many suggestions made in committee, but the fundamental changes we put forward have not been accepted. I suppose that is the reason we are engaged in a very important debate in that regard.
Of course, members of the NDP will applaud the fact that those fundamental changes have not been accepted because they are together with the Liberals on the Constitution. However, with respect to the Judges Act I suspect they will beat their chests and say they opposed the government, and that this is an example of a Tory-Liberal alliance. On more important issues the NDP supports the Liberals right down the line with no exceptions. I wanted to make that preliminary point of a non-controversial nature before I got on with this important bill relating to the salaries of judges.
The minister was prepared to make some amendments to this legislation and to allow other amendments. He instructed government supporters on the committee to accept amendments to the pension provisions of the bill. Very simply put, the bill presented by the minister and read the second time provided certain pension provisions. Pension contributions by judges were to be abolished, with the exception of nominal contributions for indexing purposes. At second reading I and other members of my party spoke in opposition to that proposal. We felt it was possibly inappropriate in terms of the precedent it might set and in view of demands and requests being made by other groups in society.
Second, it seemed to me that the salary increases proposed by the Minister of Justice in themselves sufficiently reflected a reasonable increase in the benefits to be paid to judges. The amounts proposed by the government were double those proposed by the minister's predecessor, Senator Flynn. Because of this we felt a pension contribution was appropriate.
The status quo will remain with respect to pension contributions, and the net position, quite frankly, will not be to the disadvantage of judges when we consider tax implications and the deductibility of contributions. The original proposal made by Senator Flynn when he was minister of justice was an increase of $6,500 over a period of two years. This bill provides for an increase of some $13,000 over a period of two years for, if I may use the term, the average judge. The increase will be somewhat more from chief justices and associate chief judges. However, essentially that is the increase under this legislation.
In his remarks at third reading the minister said that judges' salaries are a unique responsibility of Parliament. He made
Judges Act
reference to the fact that under Section 100 of the British North America Act the salaries, allowances and pensions of judges of the superior, district and county courts are fixed and provided by the Parliament of Canada.
That leads me to make one observation made in the committee which I again bring to the attention of the minister. That is not absolutely true. A number of other public servants are affected. Their salaries are tied to judges' salaries. Some mention was made in the committee hearings that the Chief Electoral Officer, the Auditor General and other important senior officials who serve Parliament and the people of Canada have their salaries tied directly to judges' salaries. By virtue of the device of tying more and more public servants' salaries to judges' salaries, we may be getting away from the strict meaning of the BNA Act. I think each of these responsibilities should be judged on its own merits.
Perhaps it is now time for us to look at the concept put forward by my distinguished colleague, the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert), in terms of an executive remuneration tribunal. Such a tribunal could be established by the government. It could have the responsibility of looking at the adequacy of compensation paid to senior public officials of the type I have mentioned. Perhaps this could be done rather than continuing the present haphazard and casual way of dealing with these matters in terms of trying to find appropriate salary levels for various public officials.
I commend the minister for taking the step of providing for a review of judges' salaries by what I hope will be an effective and independent commission. One of the things we in Parliament can do is look at these matters and make assessments, but it is helpful to have people expert in the field who can spend the time to examine the requirements and adequacy of compensation, particularly for judges, to report to us and be subject to the scrutiny and cross-examination of members of Parliament through our committee system.
The minister has indicated that he would be receptive on two accounts to have the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs look at the report of these people who will be advising him regarding compensation. I remind the minister that during the course of the committee hearings he undertook to establish a committee to examine the whole question of the pension contributions of judges and to report to him. I am sure he will do that before too long. He also undertook to have that committee appear before the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs so that Members of Parliament will have the opportunity to examine that committee's conclusions and the bases upon which it arrives at those conclusions.
I am not sure I heard the minister's remarks at third reading correctly, but 1 think he said judges received their last increase in 1975. If he checks the record, he will see that they received their last increase in 1977. His predecessor, the Hon. Ron Basford, brought forward legislation respecting salary increases. There has been one increase since 1975, and that was in 1977.

The position our party has taken with respect to this bill is that we question the salary increase. We were particularly concerned about the non-contributory pension aspect of it. As 1 pointed out-the minister also referred to this in his remarks-studies and recommendations have been made with respect to judicial compensation. The Casgrain report was completed and referred by the minister to the Canadian Bar Association, and the Dorfman report was prepared as an advisory report for the Minister of Justice and his department. In addition, there was a third report which was prepared for the judicial compensation committee of the Canadian judges' conference.
In each of these committees suggestions and recommendations were made with respect to increases in judges' salaries. The Casgrain report suggested increases of some $5,000 for each of the years 1979 and 1980. The Dorfman report suggested salary increases of $3,500 on April 1, 1979 and the same on April 1, 1980; and it seems to me that the judicial compensation committee of the Canadian judges' conference concurred in 1980 with the Casgrain recommendation.
What we have proposed in this bill is that an increase in excess of the amount recommended by any one of those committees be made in judges' salaries, so we are not shortchanging the judges by any means if this bill is passed. They are receiving substantially more than was recommended by any of these three committees. The second point, however, the non-contributory part of the pension, causes serious concern to members of our party and members of the NDP. Also, I am satisfied that this matter was of considerable concern to a substantial number of members on the government side. There was receptivity in the committee from all sides of the House to the conclusion to which the minister finally arrived. The minister said he would allow the provisions with respect to a non-contributory pension to be voted down and deleted from the bill, but he would have these provisions examined independently and brought back to Parliament once he had received the committee report and had a chance to analyse what might be the most appropriate course to follow.
I have made reference to the fact that my colleague, the hon. member for Edmonton West, has spoken from time to time about the whole process of determining compensation for judges. Unfortunately, he is not in the House today-he has important business in his constituency-but he has spoken to me about this matter and indicated that he continues to be interested in it. He wishes me to remind the minister that for many years now he has advocated the establishment of a remuneration review tribunal. He understands the restrictions and restraints imposed upon us by Section 100 of the British North America Act which give Parliament the mandate to set the salaries, benefits, pensions and allowances of judges, and so he understands that there are some difficulties with respect to having an independent review tribunal. On the other hand, he is still of the opinion that some method of investigation of an independent nature should be found. He will continue to put this view forward whenever the opportunity to do so arises again.
On second reading of the bill, I pointed out the importance which, I think, all of us understand must be placed on the role which an independent judiciary plays under the two systems of common law which exist in our country. As we continue debate on the Constitution and talk about a charter of rights, which will come sooner or later-one is not sure of the exact time when it will arrive in Canada-one realizes the important role which the judiciary will play.
The role of the judiciary will be very important in terms of the future of our country. It is important to have a judiciary which is representative of the people of our country and which will have the competence to deal, in an intelligent manner, with the interpretation of an entrenched bill of rights. Because it seems to me that when one looks at the experience of other jurisdictions where there is an entrenched bill of rights, one finds that the quality of the judges and their political outlook is very important in the interpretation of the rights of the people of those countries, just as it will be in the interpretation of the rights of Canadians in years to come. Again I say to the minister that the suggestions he has received with respect to the appointment of judges and to the whole process by which judges are appointed must be a consideration in terms of the policy and the practice which have taken place and will take place in our country.
Under our parliamentary system, the Minister of Justice and the government have responsibility for the appointment of judges, as periodically they have to face the voter and justify the kinds of appointments they make to the judiciary, along with other aspects of their policies, during their mandate. But in this instance, when we are moving now toward a system with an entrenched charter of rights, it becomes important for parliamentarians in particular and for the people in the country to know what the attitudes, opinions, and, quite frankly, the philosophy of the judges to be appointed will be, because the courts will be required to adjudicate upon the rights of the citizens of our country.
If we look south of the 49th parallel to see what has transpired in terms of the experience of the U.S. Supreme Court, which is the final court of appeal in that country, as we will have to look at our own Supreme Court, we see that there has been a transformation in the course of the last ten years from what was described as a Liberal Warren court to what is now described as a more Conservative, constructionist court of Chief Justice Berger. I am not commenting at all about the quality of judgments, which remains always high; but if one were to examine the decisions made with respect to the U.S. Bill of Rights and the rights available to U.S. citizens and examine what subtle transformations have taken place of certain of those fundamental rights, it would be important to understand that the composition of the Supreme Court of Canada will be a matter of interest and importance to us because of the fact that the court will have a substantial say in what the rights of the individual citizens are. What I say to the minister is that the quality and independence of the judiciary

is important, particularly now when we are moving forward toward an entrenched bill of rights.
Another aspect of this matter to which he may want to give serious consideration is finding a broader basis of consultation with respect to the appointment of judges. With regard to competence, 1 made some suggestions about the fact that the advice of the provincial law societies is not sufficiently taken into account. The minister has agreed to consider my suggestions, and I compliment him for this on behalf of members on this side.
Law societies are involved in the day-to-day administration of their membership in each province. It would be an important improvement in the consultative process of the minister and his officials with respect to judicial appointments if they relied more frequently on the recommendations of provincial bar associations and law societies. I am not in any way diminishing the importance of the role of the Canadian Bar Association. I am not suggesting for a moment that those people do not have great ability or are not of assistance to the minister.
The minister has often pointed out that he is a lawyer from Shawinigan, so he will understand that the Canadian Bar Association tends to represent the larger metropolitan areas of the country. Often rural lawyers are overlooked because they are not known to the lawyers in the bigger cities. I am not suggesting that there is any sort of conspiracy. The people who are involved in the day-to-day administration of the law societies know the competent lawyers within their provinces. They know better the abilities of rural practitioners or the people who are not involved in larger firms. I simply say to the minister, by way of constructive suggestion, that he should try to create a structure within his office and his consultative process whereby provincial bar associations will be consulted more frequently.
We have reservations with respect to the amount recommended in the bill in terms of total salary increases. We think they are quite adequate, if not more than adequate.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to take part in third reading debate on this important bill, one which comes before Parliament very rarely. As the hon. member for Saskatoon West (Mr. Elnatyshyn) indicated, I believe it was in 1977 that the Judges Act last came before Parliament.
As other members have indicated, there are three major elements to the bill in its present form. There is an increase in the number of judges to be appointed; there is a substantial salary increase; and in the original bill there was provision for the elimination of contributory pensions by judges. 1 should like to deal briefly with each of those elements of the bill.
We support the first element, which is not controversial, that is, to respond to the concerns of provincial attorneys general and increase the number of judges in several Canadian provinces as well as in the two territories.
I spoke of my concerns in my second reading speech on December 1 and also in committee with respect to the appointment process of the federal judiciary, to which the hon. member for Saskatoon West alluded. It is particularly important to examine carefully how the federal judiciary is being appointed. There is no question that there have been substantial improvements in the appointments process in recent years. The blatantly political appointments have largely, but certainly not completely, come to an end.
For example, one need only look at recent appointments in the province of Saskatchewan to see that that day is not yet completely over. I am not suggesting for a moment that politicians should be excluded from access to the judiciary, but I am suggesting that there is a remarkable coincidence between the political stripe of lawyers and appointments to the bench. It is not as bad as it used to be, but the practice certainly still goes on.
One need only look at the recent appointments to the citizenship court of this country. The three most recent appointments were the wife of a former Liberal cabinet minister, the secretary of a former Liberal cabinet minister and a former Liberal cabinet minister. Unfortunately there are still practices of that nature in the federal bench; we want them to come to an end quickly.
We do not believe the present consultative process with the Canadian Bar Association, which in many ways is a big city, old boys' network, is adequate or satisfactory. I emphasize "old boys' network" because members of the House should know that there are no women on the Canadian Bar Association committee. The hon. member for Saskatoon West suggested that our judiciary should represent the people of the country. At the present time the committee of the Canadian Bar Association is comprised of men. There are 17 judges who are to be appointed. There are many qualified women who are lawyers in the country. There are many more qualified women

March 6, 1981
Judges Act
in recent years because the number of women graduates is far greater than it was a few years ago. 1 suggest to the Minister of Justice (Mr. Chretien) that the next 17 appointments he makes pursuant to these provisions should be women. There are qualified women from coast to coast who should be taking these positions. I urge the minister to appoint women to all 17 positions. Also 1 urge the minister, as I have urged him before, to make his next appointment to the Supreme Court of Canada the first woman Supreme Court justice.
The hon. member for Saskatoon West talked of his concerns about the appointment process. We believe that this process should be opened up, not just to the law societies, as was suggested by the hon. member for Saskatoon West, but perhaps to an independent commission in each province with representatives from the community at large. I am referring to those people who are affected by the day-to-day decisions of the judiciary: representatives of the labour movement and representatives of the community at large, not just representatives of the legal profession. It could be similar to what is known as the Missouri plan in the United States. We must substantially improve the appointments process in this country.
As I said, we want to ensure that far more women are appointed. Historically a Conservative government has never in the history of this country appointed a woman to the federal court bench. We know that must change. We have concerns about the appointments process. I hope the minister will examine carefully these concerns in the months ahead.
The second provision in the original bill was one with respect to pensions. The Minister of Justice was president of the treasury board when the bill which required judges to contribute to their own pension plans was brought in. We know the former Conservative minister of justice wanted to eliminate this contributory pension plan provision. We are pleased to see the Minister of Justice accede to the very strong urgings of this party, of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) and others, who have urged the minister to reinstate the fundamental principle that the judiciary should contribute to their pensions just as all other Canadians do. We are pleased to see the minister drop those provisions of the bill in response to, as I say, our urgings and also the urgings of the Conservative Party, as well as a number of members of the Liberal caucus. The minister was responsive in that area and we appreciate that very much. We welcome the fact that the minister resisted a very powerful and yet invisible lobby of the judiciary in this country in doing that. As I say, we welcome the fact that those provisions have been dropped.
I say very frankly to the minister, through you, Mr. Speaker, that the suggestion that there should be yet another committee set up to study this question is simply a waste of the taxpayers' money. The Dorfman commission, the Canadian Bar Association and the Ministry of Justice have examined this question. We have all the evidence we need. 1 suggest that to appoint a high-priced lawyer to examine this question once again is a waste of the taxpayers' money. I say without any
equivocation whatsoever, Mr. Speaker, that there is no doubt that if this provision is brought back to this Parliament, we intend very vigorously to oppose it, as we do now.
The next major provision in the bill is a provision with respect to salary increases. This matter was touched upon by the hon. member for Saskatoon West. I believe that Canadians who are paying their taxes and who are paying these salaries should know just how rich these increases are. For example, a county court judge in Canada will have an increase in his or her salary from the present level of $47,000 a year to $65,000 a year, which is an increase of 38 per cent. A Court of Appeal judge or a Supreme Court judge at the federal level will have an increase in salary from $54,000 to $70,000-a very substantial increase. A Supreme Court of Canada justice will receive an increase in salary from the present level of $64,000 to $81,000. That increase will be effective to almost a year ago, to April 1, 1980. In just a few weeks there will be a further increase under the provisions of this bill. I will give only one example. The salaries of Supreme Court justices at the provincial level will go from $54,000 a year to $74,900 a year.
We believe that this package, in so far as it affects salaries, is excessively rich. We recognize that the judiciary must be adequately compensated. We recognize their important role in Canadian society. But we also say this: frankly, one of the arguments that is made, and perhaps the most persuasive argument, for these very substantial and excessive salary increases is that lawyers are paid very high salaries. We are told that lawyers are paid $80,000 or $90,000 a year, or $100,000 or $200,000 at the senior levels. We are told that we cannot get judges to accept a substantial cut in their pay. Very frankly, what I say the problem is, Mr. Speaker, is that lawyers in this country are overpaid. That is the problem.

I suggest that it is intolerable that in this day and age there is such affluence in the midst of such poverty.

We find the provisions for salary increases excessive. We are concerned with the fact that these salaries will be increased by 7 per cent each year. When you are at that high a salary level, that 7 per cent increase means $5,000 or $6,000 a year. This will simply increase the spread between the rich and the poor in this country. Again, we find that unacceptable.
I conclude by saying that we certainly recognize the fundamental role of the judiciary, one which must uphold the principle of the rule of law in this country. We recognize the role of a judiciary which must make decisions on such vital matters as the liberty of the subject, on how to sentence in very complex criminal matters, deciding such important questions in civil matters as who is to have custody of children and what is in the best interests of a child. We have concerns with respect to the failure of our prison system, in the hope that the judiciary might become more aware of that failure and be more innovative in their sentencing practices.
While there has been a significant improvement in this bill with respect to the restoration of the contributory element of the pension and the provisions with respect to salary increases, which are simply too rich, and while we recognize the importance of the judiciary, we will be opposing this bill at third reading.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to make some very brief remarks with respect to this legislation, since there was some distortion left on the record by the hon. member who just spoke. The first distortion had to do with the range of the application of this particular piece of legislation. It applies to federally-appointed judges, superior court judges, but it does not apply to citizenship court judges, which though they are honourable and estimable appointments within the community, are not within the classification of judges being dealt with by this bill. That is the first point.
The hon. member was correct; the bill deals with increases in the numbers of judges in various places. I am happy to note that he was not arguing that this is not necessary in certain areas. Because of changes in the organization of Canadian society and the fact that it is becoming more complex as government intervenes to a greater degree in the lives of individuals, the work of judicial tribunals is necessary and there is bound to be an increase. I make no comment on the workload of judges, except to say that it is increasing in certain areas and in some areas it is not. The federal government has no alternative but to look at the necessity of increasing the size of the bench from time to time.
I am glad to see the Minister of Justice (Mr. Chretien) agrees that we should remove the problem of pensions from the bill and have that dealt with in another manner. I think that is in keeping with the atmosphere that ought to prevail in the House when we are dealing with judges, who do not have the right to speak for themselves but depend upon Parliament and this system to speak for them. Therefore, it behooves Parliament and all parliamentarians on every side of the House to judge the issue on its merits and not on the basis of prejudice and possible preconceptions, which might be deemed to be right in the mind of the speaker but are woefully wrong in terms of the work of the legal profession.
That brings me to the question of salaries for judges. The hon. member for Burnaby (Mr. Robinson), who has just spoken, said that the package is excessively rich. I do not know

March 6, 1981
Judges Act
whether it is excessively rich or not, but from my experience in government I do know that there is some difficulty in attracting the best to the bench. The difference between our lives and the life of a judge is that we in Parliament can take part in the community, can involve ourselves in many organizations, and indeed we seek to do so. We do not have to exercise the same care that a judge must when choosing his associates. We do not have to withdraw from many associations, and we do not lose the right, which other citizens have, to speak out on public matters. A judge loses all those rights. I hear my hon. friend from South Shore (Mr. Crouse) saying a judge even loses the right to vote, the most fundamental right enjoyed by any citizen.
When a person considers whether he will go to the bench, he considers many factors: whether he enjoys the study of law; whether he is prepared to endure the tedium of the law-there are tediums in all professions, but particularly with the bench. He also has to decide whether he is prepared to give up some rights that my friend and I take for granted. I think those are tremendous considerations for any person. He must also consider his family.
We must consider our duty to ensure that the judge, or whatever court we are dealing with, is adequately compensated so that with respect to the vicissitudes of life he will never put himself in a compromising position.

That was the intent of the hon. member for Burnaby (Mr. Robinson). We are pleased that this bill is being debated today and we expect it will go through, but it is about time. The hon. member for Nepean-Carleton (Mr. Baker) was right when he said it is difficult to criticize judges because they cannot reply. They can reply through lawyers who are prominent members of the bar, however. If I say anything that judges object to, I am sure they can take that route as I think they will be listening to and reading this debate today.
In British Columbia, where I am a member of the bar, there have been some problems recently with judges getting into trouble with the law. I do not want to go into details but I think I should note that people who do not have the privileged position in society that lawyers and judges have, expect judges to be above running into problems with the law. I think judges in my province especially have noted that in the last year.
In the last Parliament I raised the question of the difficulties that arose following the resignation of the former chief justice of the court of appeal in British Columbia and I want to clarify that question. I did not raise the question to deal with that specific matter as, frankly, I think the judge in that case suffered enough. What I wanted to deal with was the discipline procedure for judges. I think the Minister of Justice (Mr. Chretien) should look into that matter. The judge in question in British Columbia resigned, so no inquiry could be carried out in that case. That may or may not be proper but the public was never really satisfied that no wrongdoing went on. I do not think there was any wrongdoing but 1 do not know. I would suggest that a prominent lawyer could be appointed to look into the situation-not to deal with the activities of that particular man but to then be in a position to tell the public there was no wrongdoing. I think the public would have felt
Judges Act
better, and I know I would, if such a report had been brought forward. I leave that suggestion with the Minister of Justice.
Now 1 come to the matter of appointments and here I depart slightly from the position taken by the hon. member for Nepean-Carleton. We know that when the Liberals are in, a lot of Liberals are appointed to the bench, and when the Conservatives are in government, Conservatives are appointed to the bench. So far this party has not been in a position to make appointments! The hon. member for Nepean-Carleton put his finger on the problem, as did the hon. member for Burnaby, that political people should not be excluded from judicial life but politics should not be the first criteria for appointment. I would suggest to the Minister of Justice that future appointments be vetted by a special committee of the House of Commons so that qualifications could be examined and gross political appointments eliminated.
I think there is a need for reform in the manner of making appointments. As the hon. member for Nepean-Carleton said, women are ready to be appointed to the bench and the government should appoint them. There are other types of lawyers as well, who could be appointed. In the last 10 or 15 years lawyers who have gone into community law, administrative law, and the teaching profession would make fine judges and I think the minister should expand the base of appointment. It is important that we have judges from all walks of legal life.
I wanted to bring up something now that is not in the bill. I refer to conditions in the courts. At the present time we have a strange court system in Canada. A difference is made between county court judges and supreme court judges in the bill. I could never understand the rationale behind that distinction. I do not even understand why there is a federal court. I think a lot of money is wasted by having different courts. We should have one superior court and one supreme court in each province.
The hon. member for Burnaby alluded to reforms that need to be made in the legal system and to different kinds of law. Judges are only part of the system. I practised family and domestic law and know there needs to be reform in the courts in that area. I was pleased that with the co-operation of the federal government we were able to set up a model family court in British Columbia.
I was disappointed that the Minister of Justice did not include the right of counsel as a real right of counsel in the charter of human rights. That is not only the right to have a lawyer if you can pay but the right to have a lawyer if you cannot afford to pay; in other words, legal aid for people who cannot afford a lawyer and the right to that legal aid. I fought and lost a case on that very point in the court of appeal in British Columbia. I hope in the near future in this country we will have the real right to counsel; that means being provided with a lawyer if you cannot afford one. I think any judge would say that it is helpful when both parties are well represented by counsel.
I have made some criticisms of judges, Mr. Speaker, but we have had some great ones. I think of Mr. Justice Hall of

March 6, 1981
Judges Act
Saskatchewan; 1 think of Chief Justice Duff of British Columbia; 1 think of Justice Rand from the maritimes; of Justice Laskin from Ontario and I know there have been some excellent judges from Quebec.
I am a member of the bar of the Northwest Territories, Mr. Speaker. There we had perhaps one of the greatest judges of all, an authentic Canadian hero, Mr. Justice Sissons, the first judge of the north, whose area of jurisdiction reached the North Pole. He was succeeded by another great man, Mr. Justice Morrow who unfortunately died last year. I wish to pay tribute to him in the House today.
One of the things that Mr. Justice Sissons said, and this was taken up by Justice Morrow, was that justice should go to every man's house. When he said that, it meant taking justice to everyone in the north. It was a very difficult area to administer but he did it. I think if we carry that tradition on, this country will be well served.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, all hon. members who have spoken have pointed to the fact that judges will have to deal with the charter of human rights.
I want to conclude by quoting words, not from a Canadian judge, but from an American judge, William O. Douglas who used the words "a judge should have courage and humanity in his or her decisions." I say to judges in Canada who will be interpreting the charter of human rights that I hope, as I am sure other members of this House do, they will interpret that charter and deal with the fundamental problems of human rights in this country with courage and with humanity.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, this is a subject which has concerned me for many years. I could speak at length on it, but I shall be very brief. I want to say at the outset that the hon. member for Nepean-Carleton (Mr. Baker) said one thing with which I fully agree, namely, that we should approach this subject on its merits. speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader

speechtext:
We live on the same street here in Ottawa, but on opposite sides of that street.
I suppose the thing which has bothered me all my life about our society is that those who have get more and those who do not have lose even what they have got. I just do not like it. Time and time again we find the money for massive increases to those in the upper economic reaches. But those who are down lower lose what they have through inflation, through taxes and through the increased prices they have to pay. I hope some day to see this situation turned around.
We have made some improvements over the years. I could make a speech in which I could almost boast of the improvements we have made in social legislation during the decades I have been in this Parliament, but we are still ready first to give more to those who have, and offer only sympathy and concern for those who have not. As my friend, the hon. member for Burnaby (Mr. Robinson) pointed out, this bill is going to push some judges who are now in the lower brackets into the $60,000 bracket. It will push some into the $70,000 bracket and it will push others into the $80,000 bracket. On top of that, there is an automatic 7 per cent annual increase. When you are talking about a salary of $70,000, a 7 per cent increase amounts to $4,900. If you are in the $80,000 bracket, a 7 per cent increase amounts to $5,600.
These figures are more, just by way of an increase, than the total amount which is available to a pensioner who draws both old age security and the full amount of the guaranteed income supplement. Most of our senior citizens, and this means most of the 2 million people over the age of 65, are struggling at or just below the poverty line. We have many others, particularly women, in the 55 to 65 age bracket, those unattached who would be well off if they could get up to the poverty line who are having a difficult time. Then there are the working poor and the unemployed. These are problems which face our society. If we want to call ourselves democratic, advanced and progressive, if we want to have a Canadian identity to be proud of, these are the areas in which we should be working.
I cannot bring myself to believe that it is the right thing in the face of these problems to keep on giving massive increases to those who are at the top. If some hon. members suspect that because I feel that way about the increases in this bill I may have even more to say about certain other increases if they are brought before this House-I need not mention them as every member knows what I am talking about, I can tell them they will hear from me when that time comes.
I agree with everything that has been said today about the importance of our judiciary. I agree with the things that have been said about the place they hold in society. I Still think that is worth something. I still think, if I may go back that far, that there was something to the idea in Edward Bellamy's "Looking Backward", who said that those who had to do the dirtiest and the meanest jobs should get paid more than those who had the privilege of doing the delightful and the enjoyable jobs. That is why I say to the hon. member from Nepean-Carleton we are on different wavelengths and, although we live on the same street, we are on opposite sides of the street. I think this is important. While I do not want to spin out this debate, I do feel 1 should state again that I am opposed to the way we approach these things. I think the suggestion that we will do the other afterward is not enough because it never happens. I am more concerned for the others, and, with all of the respect I have for the judiciary, I am opposed to this bill. I shall be voting no.
