speakerposition: Minister of Transport
subsubtopic: CONCURRENCE IN FOURTH REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the transport committee has tabled its fourth report and the chairman, the hon. member for Northumberland-Miramichi (Mr. Dionne), is now asking for concurrence.
I must commend the committee for doing an excellent job and I wish I had more time to elaborate on that but unfortunately I don't.
Among other subjects the committee studied the activities of the CN and two full days were devoted to questioning the president of this Crown corporation, Mr. Robert Bandeen. Most of the questions had to do with the decision of CN Express to close about half of its 70 offices located here and there throughout the country and, particularly, to close 10-

March 6, 1981
CN Express
we will see in a moment that this has been reduced to 8-out of a total of 15 in the maritime provinces.
Unhappy about that decision, the committee has recommended, and I quote:
That the government consider the advisability of requiring Canadian National Railways to continue the CN Express Service at the minimum of the 1979 level.
Consequently, Mr. Speaker, I reviewed the whole question with Mr. Bandeen and his officials. We examined the suggestion made in the recommendation and, as you are probably aware, Mr. Speaker, adjustments were made to the previous decisions, particularly as regards Charlottetown and Sydney.
That is what I now want to go over rapidly in seven or eight minutes in the hope that the House will agree that at least the spirit of the recommendation of the transport committee has been respected.

Let us look at the facts. First, why the reduction of terminals at CN Express? Notwithstanding CN's numerous efforts over the years at reorganizing, controlling costs and introducing new services, such as Rapidex, volume declined from 24 million shipments in the 1950s to seven million in 1980, a period of 30 years. Second, CN's share of this market decreased to 5 per cent of less than truckload shipments and 2 per cent of small parcels. That is not the massive service that some people talk about when referring to CN Express. Third, financial losses have grown accordingly; $53 million in 1980 and a total of $205 million over the last five years.
What were the options for CN Express? The first was to continue unchanged with the decreasing market share and increasing losses. That would have affected the viability of other operations of CN. However, with the prevailing philosophy with regard to commercial Crown corporations, CN might or would have been expected to turn to the government and ask for a compensating subsidy, as has done with CN Marine.
Having such a subsidy might have been justified in the "national" interest, in the interest of all of us as users of these services. 1 am not opposed philosophically to subsidies. There are instances when they can be justified.
CN did not think so in this case, and I agreed with them. 1 ask why? Simply because many of these services that CN is rendering are now performed by other carriers in a commercially viable fashion at reasonable rates. That is the basis of the decision 1 made.
In recent years we have had almost a cultural change in this sector of transportation. Because of the revolutionary development of highways and of the trucking industry, CN has suffered from fierce competition. In most of Canada, aggressive private trucking firms have taken over the market from CN Express to a substantial extent, and hence the decline to 5 per cent and 2 per cent referred to already.
There are, for example, ten such trucking firms in Amherst, 28 in Sydney and they specialize in certain types of operations. They do a good job. There is no hope that CN Express will ever come back to its past predominant position.
The other option, the one CN took, was to redefine its role in the express business; leave to private truckers what they can do better, that is handle small parcels, concentrate on what CN Express does best, the so-called less than truckload type of shipment, integrate CN operations with local trucking firms to ensure adequacy of service, and cut down the number of outlets or terminals. That is what I as Minister of Transport accepted.
My acceptance was not unconditional. It depended on three conditions being realized. The first was the protection to be given to employees. That has been done to a substantial extent. Acceptable terms have been negotiated with the union and an agreement was signed last November.
As we know, the workers have three choices: retraining, relocation and retirement. Between 80 per cent and 90 per cent of the affected employees will enjoy these options. Most of the others are eligible for severance pay. In the present situation, there are about 5,000 employees of CN Express. About 1,000 will be affected by the policy of redefinition. The numbers change slightly every day as employees avail themselves of the choices offered. At this time 400 have made their intentions known. About 200, half the number, have found jobs elsewhere in CN, 100 have opted for early retirement and 100 have resigned, having found jobs elsewhere. In many cases they will benefit from the severance pay I referred to. Those who joined CN Express recently are not entitled to the same advantages as those who have been employed there five, 10, 15 or 25 years.
The second condition was that the communities would continue to receive express service. This is being done. As we see in their very interesting ads in the newspapers, CN Express takes the responsibility for a system. CN Express takes this responsibility by interlining and contracting with local truck companies. It does so by staying in a certain community when no one else can ensure service, for example in Churchill, Manitoba. In recent advertisements CN has stated: "CN will still be serving all its existing points." But it will be doing so in a way which makes more sense in today's market. CN takes the responsibility for providing service. It then signs contracts with trucking companies to ensure that that responsibility is carried out.
Following the review recommended by the committee two special cases were identified. I referred to them in the House on February 4. The first one is Charlottetown, where we decided to keep the terminal open because closing it would have left the province without any direct CN Express presence. The second exception was the Sydney office which was kept open simply because of the exceptionally poor employment situation in that area at this time. The promise CN Express has made-and for which I presume I am the guarantor-is to keep those two offices open until mid-1983 when the situation will be reviewed again. Instead of ten, only-and I know "only" is not the right expression-eight offices in the Atlantic provinces are closing.
March 6, 1981

The third condition which I imposed was that the rate structure which would result from the redefinition would be reasonable. Of course, in the future there will be increases, but already a first round of changes have taken place. By way of comment I can only refer to the point that the general picture will not be affected with respect to the express system as a whole. I can only comment on the analysis made by the Atlantic Provinces Transportation commission, a group charged with the protection of the interests of shippers, in which comparisons of 530 rates established that as a consequence of the new program 50 per cent of the rates stayed the same, 30 per cent increased and 20 per cent decreased. If I had more time, I would quote from this analysis at length because it includes some very important aspects.
So there it is. I have almost exhausted my ten minutes. I have tried to explain the circumstances as best I could in such a short period of time, especially as a former academic. I certainly understand the reservations of the committee, and I understand the importance of the recommendations it made to me. I hope I have come out of this in an honourable fashion. I hope also that the public at large and particularly the employees of CN Express will find that they are duly protected either as users of the services or as employees of CN Express. I hope my colleagues in the House will acknowledge that I have paid attention to the recommendations of the committee.

subsubtopic: CONCURRENCE IN FOURTH REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am glad the minister was here in the House to put forward the position of the government.
This debate is taking place in this House because of a motion put by my colleague, the hon. member for Regina West (Mr. Benjamin), at the committee level. It is because of his concern about cutbacks in CN Express service that we have the opportunity to debate this today.
This is a very important matter. There is a fundamental policy question here. To listen to the minister, one might think that these cutbacks in express service are rational and a move in the right direction. The problem is that the cutbacks result from a fundamentally flawed policy of the government. I refer to a letter which a former minister of transport, Otto Lang, wrote on January 13, 1977, which laid out the government's attitude and policy with respect to the CNR. It quite simply says that the CNR is a commercial enterprise and must be run as a commercial enterprise, and that the real criteria for the operation of this service must be a balanced book and a profit margin. I fundamentally reject that approach. It is the belief of members of my party that the government has a responsibility for transportation services across the country. One of the reasons we have a public corporation such as the CNR is to serve the public and not simply to make a profit.
We should remember that the CNR was first formed from a collection of private companies which at that time were bankrupt. The public brought them together and made a viable enterprise of them in order to serve the people. Now that this corporation is operating efficiently and effectively, the government wants to separate the profit-making parts of it from
CN Express
those parts which require revenues and subsidies, so the government can either turn over the profit-making parts to the private sector or simply justify cutbacks in services. Behind this cutback in service, behind this loss of jobs and behind this loss of services to communities is a fundamentally flawed government policy. First and foremost the policy should emphasize service to the community and to the country rather than treating the CNR simply as a profit-making venture.
As he was speaking, the minister spoke about the losses faced by the CNR. We believe those losses are exaggerated and that the amount of money which is said to be lost by CN Express is far out of proportion. For example, the figure I have here indicates that the loss for 1980 was $51 million. I understand this includes $24.4 million charged to CN Express by other CN departments. It is my understanding that if there were no CN Express, CN would not save this full amount of $24 million. The amount charged to CN Express by the other departments is exaggerated because it includes overhead and other items which would have to be in place in any event.
Not only is the amount of money which supposedly would be saved, if we did not have this express service, exaggerated, but we suspect as well that prices can be raised deliberately and service levels withdrawn in order to discourage customers. For example, let us look at past experience in Saskatchewan. Before the removal of service, rates from Regina to Fort Qu'Appelle went up by some 94 per cent; rates from Regina to Kamsack went up by some 87 per cent; and rates from Regina to Prince Albert went up by some 52 per cent. Before these massive increases CN Express was charging the same as other companies. With these massive increases CN has overcharged and thereby reduced its own share of the market. CN did not take advantage of the full revenue potential for its service that existed. We feel the losses stated by CN for CN Express are exaggerated and out of line.
Another aspect of this matter which concerns us greatly is that of lay-offs. The minister referred to that. He is right when he says he has done something in this respect, and he deserves credit. He is keeping open the two terminals at Sydney and Charlottetown. He has done something to alleviate the situation regarding loss of jobs, but there still is a large employment loss. My understanding is that another 1,100 jobs will be lost. One quarter of those jobs will be lost in Atlantic Canada. That is a considerable loss of employment, particularly at a time when the economy is not creating new jobs rapidly, and that is to understate the matter. These lost jobs will hurt the communities where these jobs have existed until now. They will hurt the heads of households who have to support their families, pay for heating, food, children's clothing and other essentials. There is a human side to this which must not be overlooked.
In light of the fact that this cutback is not justified, it is hard to understand why the government is proceeding in this direction, other than that it chose to treat the CNR as if it

March 6, 1981
CN Express
were a private profit-making corporation rather than the public utility which it really is.
Another important aspect of this cutback in the CN Express service is that the railways made commitments with regard to the provision of their services. In other words, when they moved from a rail service to a trucking service they made certain commitments about maintaining service. I heard the minister echoing this once again when he spoke just now. He is saying that when we move from the CN Express trucking service to the private sector trucking service, somehow there will be no loss of service. I take these assurances with a grain of salt, particularly in light of the previous commitments by the railways. For example, on December 7, 1971, CP Rail undertook the following:
CP Rail undertakes through the CSC to provide a service equal or superior to the service presently being provided under the station agent system.
The commitment of CNR was as follows:
Right from the day a servocentre goes on stream the service provided to customers from it will be at least equal to that which is available through conventional facilities, and in many cases immediately superior to that now available.
These are commitments made by railways that their service would remain at the same level, and yet now we hear about further cutbacks. When they moved from rail to road, they assured the people that the service would stay at the same level. Now they are pulling back on express services and we are being assured that these will be provided by the private sector. It is difficult to take those assurances seriously.
Finally, I want to come back to the fact that the most important point about this cutback in the CNR Express service is that the government is following a fundamentally misguided policy of treating CNR as if it were a private commercial venture when, in fact, it is a public utility. These cutbacks in express services provided by a public utility are unjustified. They remind us of cutbacks in passenger services and in branch lines.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to speak briefly on the matter before the House simply to reemphasize the comments I made when this matter came before the committee. We in Nova Scotia look upon the day of November 5, 1980, when all of us as representatives of that area received the notice from the Canadian Transport Commission, as black Wednesday because it was truly a shocker to all of us, especially to me as Member for Parliament for South Shore. We were informed at that time that the agency positions located at Rockingham, Windsor Junction, Upper Mus-quodoboit, Chester, Mahone Bay, Lunenburg, Liverpool, Lockeport, Shelburne, Barrington Passage and Yarmouth were to be closed. We were told as well that the station buildings located at Upper Musquodoboit, Chester, Mahone Bay, Lunenburg, Liverpool, Lockeport, Shelburne and Barrington Passage will be put up for sale. I would remind the minister that of that list which I just placed on the record, seven out of the eight places are in my constituency, and of the previous list, seven out of 11 are in my riding. The minister states that this was due to a decline in business. He states that
the business was picked up by private companies and that there was nothing he could do about it.
Surely, Mr. Speaker, this points out the obvious fact that somewhere along the line in CN we have faulty management. The management of those operations in that area have to be at fault because in recent years there has been a gradual improvement in economic conditions along the south shore of Nova Scotia. We have had, for example, in Chester, one of the areas where operations have been curtailed and closed down, a gradual improvement of business in the Hawboldt Industries Ltd., a gradual improvement in shipbuilding, and specifically in yacht building for American interests. If the CN express had been on their toes, surely they could have received some of that business.
The same situation applies to Mahone Bay where industrial shipping is building fibreglass pipe which is shipped all over the nation and to the United States. They must bring in much of the material required. Here again, when the original service was established in the area, there was less business available than there is today. In my own home town of Lunenburg, where we have the largest fish processing plant in North America, a plant which only recently added $3 million or more to its operations by expanding its fish processing facility, obviously new business opportunities exist.
Twelve miles farther on into the town of Bridgewater, you will find the Michelin Tire Company which located there some eight or ten years ago. It is a town which has grown from about 4,000 people to over 8,000 people, double the population. Yet here we find a closing down of CN Express. If we go on to Queens County, the towns of Liverpool as well as Brooklyn, we will find located Bowaters Mersey Paper Company Limited, a very progressive company which has been expanding its operations in recent years, adding to its payroll and adding to the volume of business it conducts. Here again you find the sale of the station and a cut down in CN Express.
You could go the whole length of the south shore and see a gradual improvement, such as the location of McCloud Fisheries at Port Houton, and a new company, Polar Bear Fisheries, at Port Hebert, along with the expansion of the marine ship repair industry in Shelburne.
Some day I hope the minister will find time to come to Nova Scotia. Although he is of one political persuasion and I of another, I would gladly make myself available, if he could find the time. I would take him, not on a Cook's tour, but on a Crouse tour of the south shore which, I think, he would find informative and helpful to understanding what is happening there and what he is doing to that area. It is all very well for him to say that some employees have taken early retirement and that CN has been a good employer of these people. No one questions that, Mr. Speaker, but what we are questioning are the actions being taken by this government. The closures to which the minister is agreeing in effect are a betrayal of the terms under which Nova Scotia entered Confederation. The only argument the minister has been able to present to the House this afternoon is that this action must be taken because CN is losing a few dollars in that area. This same government
March 6, 1981

can find millions of dollars to bail out automobile companies, it can find millions of dollars for firms which really have no binding commitment on the government, as has CN and the people in our area, and they expect the government to fulfil its obligations and commitment under the terms of Confederation. At the rate we are going, it seems to me that CN is entirely forgetting Nova Scotia.
Let us consider for a minute what is happening down there. In Halifax there is the pending sale of the Hotel Nova Scotian. There is the closing of express terminals in Amherst, Port Hawkesbury, Yarmouth and Bridgewater. There is a reduction by 50 per cent of the staff of the express terminal in Sydney, a move which is nothing but a minor reprieve from the previous planned closure of that outlet. There are drastic reductions in express service in Pictou County where it appears more than 30 jobs will be lost.
The current cutbacks are not the beginning of this regressive railway tale. During recent years railway lines have been abandoned and stations have been closed. This is causing tremendous concern throughout the entire length and breadth of our province, not just along the south shore. For example, recent warnings have come to my ears from the towns of Oxford and Falmouth. Perhaps I should call them the most recent victims of the policy being approved and accepted by the present minister. iThis applies to the management of the greenhouses located in Oxford and in the Annapolis Valley near Falmouth, both of which have used CN Express to ship their products to out-of-province markets. With the curtailment of CN Express, it would appear that there is no alternative method for these people to get their products to markets in Quebec, and I believe they ship as far away as Montreal. So, these people join the large number of fresh fish plant operators in my constituency who are concerned about the manner in which they will get their fresh fish to upper Canadian markets. They have used CN Express in the past.

speakeroldname: Hon. Marc Lalonde (Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources) moved
speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
that Bill C-60, to amend the National Energy Board Act, be read the second time and referred to Committee of the Whole.
He said: Mr. Speaker, first I should like to thank the House for its co-operation in accepting the proposal to consider this bill in such an expeditious manner. I will try not to abuse the indulgence of the House, but 1 have a few comments concerning the nature of the bill. It has great significance, and it would be only fair to Canadians if I took this opportunity to put a summary on the record concerning the nature of this bill so that everyone will know exactly what it tries to do.
Therefore, it gives me great pleasure to move second reading of Bill C-60, to amend the National Energy Board Act, which received first reading by the House on February 10, 1981. The

March 6, 1981
National Energy Board Act
purpose of. this bill is to modernize the statutory procedures used by pipeline companies under federal jurisdiction to acquire lands for their pipelines.
The provisions of the bill will greatly expand the recognition of the rights of the affected land owners, not only in so far as the amount of compensation they receive is concerned, but also by providing them the right at a public hearing to inquire into the appropriateness of the route selected by the company. It is my belief that the bill I am presenting substantially incorporates all the major recommendations of the Law Reform Commission of Canada expressed in its 1975 working paper on the subject of the various expropriation powers conferred under federal statutes.
Before going any further, I wish to express my indebtedness to the Senate of Canada and to my colleague, the Hon. Senator Olson, for their invaluable work in the preparation of this bill.
Currently, the acquisition of land by pipeline companies is governed by the provisions of the Railway Act. This statute, which has not been significantly amended since 1919, has served its purpose, but no longer reflects the views of our society as to the balance that should be drawn between the public interest and the rights of the owners of private property. The Law Reform Commission has criticized the existing procedure, primarily on the ground that no opportunity is given to land owners to question the detailed route chosen by the pipeline company. It has also been criticized on the basis of a lack of codification of the types of damage which should be compensated for, a feature which is common to modern expropriation statutes, including the Expropriation Act of Canada. The present bill addresses those concerns to a degree which, I suggest, makes it one of the most fair and even-handed expropriation statutes in Canada.
I would now like to briefly describe the features of the bill. They can be divided into three main areas: first, the approval of the detailed route of the pipeline; second, the determination of the compensation payable to land owners; and third, the provision governing acquisition by the pipeline company of the right to proceed with construction where agreement has not been reached with the land owner.
Hon. members should note that all of the procedures contained in the bill will be available, not only to land owners whose property will actually be taken for the pipeline, but also to those owners of neighbouring land who will be adversely affected by the proximity of the pipeline. These owners will be notified of the intention of the company to apply to the National Energy Board for approval of its detailed route, and they will be entitled to file objections with the board. If an objection is received regarding any part of the route, the board is required to hold a hearing in that locality, at which time the land owners will have a right to be heard. The board can either alter the route of the pipeline or it can minimize the damage caused by imposing terms and conditions on the approval
which will regulate, among other things, the method and timing of acquiring the land and of constructing the pipeline.
To ensure that land owners receive fair compensation, the bill includes a list of types of damage which must be compensated for. Owners whose land will be taken will be given option as to whether they prefer to receive periodic payments, in the nature of a land rental, with the right to have the amount of these payments reviewed at five-year intervals. This option will eliminate the need which now exists to anticipate, in advance, all types of damage which may be caused to an owner by the construction of a pipeline.
As further protection, the bill ensures that every land owner will be advised of his rights under the statute before he enters into any binding contract with the company. As soon as the company identifies the land that it may need for its pipeline, it will be required to serve a notice on every owner advising not only the amount of compensation the company is offering but also explaining, in detail, the various procedures available under the act for his protection, including the right to dispute the route selected.
The procedure for determining disputes as to the amount of compensation will now be removed from the courts. Once the detailed route of the pipeline has been approved and the company is unable to reach agreement with the land owner, either party may apply to me to appoint a negotiator to assist in the bargaining. If the negotiation is unsuccessful, either party may apply to me to have the matter submitted to an arbitration committee for binding determination. Except in a case where the compensation demands of the land owner are unreasonable, the pipeline company will pay the costs of all of these proceedings, including the hearing before the National Energy Board for approval of the detailed route.
Finally, where the company is unable to conclude an agreement with the land owner, it may nevertheless acquire access to his land for construction purposes by applying to the National Energy Board. At least 30 days before this application, the company must advise the land owner of its intention to apply, and the land owner will be entitled to send written objections to the Board. In granting the company access to the land the Board can impose terms and conditions to minimize the damage caused.
Wherever a company receives such a right of entry the land owner becomes entitled to an advance payment on the compensation which will be payable to him. Any disagreement with respect to the amount or the payment of that advance can be submitted for arbitration.

Mr. Speaker, once enacted, this bill will apply to all oil and gas pipelines under federal jurisdiction whose detailed route has not been approved by the National Energy Board when the Act is implemented. Moreover, the procedure concerning the determination of the compensation will apply to land owners who have not entered into an agreement with a company and who have not yet been expropriated under the present provi-
March 6, 1981

sions. Thus, the bill will apply to the northern Foothills pipeline and the Quebec-Maritime gas pipeline extension. [English]
The Foothills Pipe Line company has indicated that if the bill should be passed into law at some point prior to the completion of the Alaska Highway Gas Project, it would be prepared to make adjustments which further reflect the new approach provided for under Bill C-60.

Consequently, quick passage of this bill will enable land owners affected by the construction of the northern pipeline to benefit from these new provisions. Finally, passage of Bill C-60 will certainly be an improvement and an undeniable advantage for land owners in Quebec, New Brunswick and Nova Scotia who will have to part with some of their lands for the construction of a gas pipeline that we have committed ourselves to complete as quickly as possible.

I trust that the House will agree with me that the bill represents a great step forward in the fair treatment of private parties affected by some of the major public interest projects on the horizon.
The implementation of these new procedures can be expected to produce certain effects on the construction of pipeline projects. First, it will produce some delay in the construction of these projects. Primarily, this will result from the requirement that hearings be held in order to approve the detailed route of a pipeline. The bill contains provisions which will ensure that these delays are no longer than is absolutely required. 1 would suggest that whatever delays are unavoidable constitute a very small price to pay for a significant improvement in the fairness of these procedures.
The bill will also produce some increase in the cost of pipeline projects. In almost all cases the companies will bear the cost of implementing these procedures. It is expected that there will be some increase in the average amount of compensation paid to each land owner. This will result from the measures taken to ensure that land owners are advised of their rights, and also from the provision for compensation for all sorts of damage, including damage suffered by land owners adjacent to the pipeline right-of-way. I know of many people in the prairies, in particular, who will be very interested in this improvement in our legislation.

I believe that we have to expect an increase in the number of arbitration cases to determine compensation in view of the relaxing of the arbitration procedure and the various provisions under which the company building a pipeline will pay the costs considered reasonable of all the proceedings started by an owner who disagrees with the amount of compensation offered.
The statistical data which I have received from the National Energy Board show that in previous cases of pipeline construction by major companies, very few compensation settlements
National Energy Board Act
were subjected to arbitration as they represent as little as 0.6 per cent of the owners involved. This figure might point to the generosity of the companies, but it also probably indicates the lack of understanding of owners concerning their rights or a reluctancy on their part to undertake costly appeal procedures about the amount of compensation granted. It seems to me that the provisions we are proposing here will help to restore the balance between the rights of the pipeline companies and those of the land owners, since the costs incurred in obtaining equitable compensation are no less of a burden for the owner than the damages he sustains.
This bill will also result in an increase in the operating cost of the pipeline once it has been built. That increase will stem from the fact that the companies will have to compensate the land owners for damages caused in the maintenance and operation of the pipeline. That aspect of the matter was somewhat overlooked in the old act, in the sense that negotiations were left entirely to the discretion of the companies and the land owners. No procedure was provided for settling claims by arbitration. I think I can say that the principles of justice and fairness demand that this type of damage not be treated any differently from those that are suffered when the pipeline is built.
Mr. Speaker, I therefore move second reading of the bill and thank all parties for their co-operation in passing this important bill in good time, for 1 feel sure it will benefit a large number of Canadians in the years to come.

Mr. Speaker, it is not my intention this afternoon to take up too much time of the House or delay the proceedings. We are very anxious and have been for a long time to ensure that this legislation passes. Farmers in western Canada who will be affected by it really want it.
There are two points I would like to bring to the attention of the minister and I assume he will agree with them. They concern the interpretation of the bill, and have been brought to our attention by the Canadian Confederation of Agriculture which represents the Unifarm in the province of Alberta which, in turn, represents the same constituency as I do. While 1 recognize there are other members involved, I do think that perhaps the constituents I represent will be more affected by this piece of legislation, because the substation where the division takes place is in my constituency and that is a fairly heavily populated part of the country. Further, it is a beef producing area, so there might be complications.
Nevertheless, I would like to bring to the attention of the minister, and I trust 1 am correct in assuming this on behalf of Unifarm and Canadian Confederation of Agriculture and the farmers in that area, that when we look at Clause 73(1) (a) (iii) we find that "the inspection, maintenance or repair of the pipeline" shall be considered for reimbursement. There is one word that has been left out. When we go back to the previous clause, it says:

March 6, 1981
National Energy Board Act
73(1) The provisions of this part that provide negotiation and arbitration procedures to determine compensation matters apply in respect of all damage caused by the pipeline of a company or anything carried by the pipeline but do not apply to
(a)	claims against a company arising out of activities of the company unless those activities are directly related to
(i)	the acquisition of lands for a pipeline,
(ii)	the construction of the pipeline, or
(iii)	the inspection, maintenance or repair of the pipeline;-
I think the word which has been omitted by oversight is the word "operations", because there could be something happening during operations which could cause problems-for instance, a leak or some other type of problem. I am sure I am correct in the assumption that the word "operations" should be incuded, because if we read Clause 74(1 )(d) it says:
(d) indemnification from all liabilities, damages, claims, suits and actions arising out of the operations of the company other than liabilities, damages, claims, suits and actions resulting from negligence or wilful misconduct of the owner of the lands;
"Operations" is included there, so I trust I am correct in the assumption that "operations" should have been included in Clause 73( l)(iii).
The other point 1 wanted to bring to the attention of the minister was with regard to the statement by the minister wherein he said that their payments will be reviewed every five years. The concern of the farmers and farm organizations relates to Clause 75.19(2) wherein it says:
(2) For the purpose of paragraph (!)(a), "market value" is the amount that would have been paid for the lands if, at the time of their taking, they had been sold in the open market by a willing seller to a willing buyer.
The point is that the farmers do not want to be tied to that point, "market value", "at the time of their taking", because 1 trust we are correct in assuming that the market value will be considered every five years, as is provided in Clause 74(l)(b) wherein it says:
(b)	review of the amount of compensation payable for acquisition of lands every five years where annual or other periodic payments have been selected;
The point we make to the minister is that when the adjustment is made every five years, the value of the land also should be taken into consideration, because as everyone knows, in these times of inflation, land values have been escalating tremendously.
So with those two points included, and if the minister can give his approval today that my assumptions are correct, I am sure that we will satisfy the farmers and the farm organizations which represent them. I recognize that sometimes these issues have to be resolved in court, and the reason I want to bring them to the attention of the House today is so that during arbitration or a court hearing the debate which has taken place today will be taken into consideration; that there is an understanding that this is how this bill will be interpreted.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am proud to stand as my party spokesman for Bill C-60, an act to amend the National Energy Board Act. This bill is like closing the door after the cattle have gotten out. In this party, we are basically satisfied with the content of the legislation,
but we are concerned that the government has waited so long to bring it in.
Last July the government forced us to accept the new pre-build of the pipeline which is going to carry natural gas to the United States. It seemed it could spare no time to get on with the job of giving our gas reserves to the Americans. At that time, Senator Olson was fully aware of the problems that could occur through the expropriation procedures. Senator Olson championed the committee through the Senate to try to bring about changes in the expropriation procedures. He introduced expropriation legislation to the Senate in the spring of 1979, after chairing the Senate pipeline committee.
In his often quoted speech introducing the legislation, the senator described the current provisions of the Railway Act as archaic, and wondered out loud about the untenable position of land owners facing expropriation under that act.
I myself am at a loss to understand how this government, knowing full well the implications of what it was doing, could go ahead with construction of the pipeline without first ensuring that the rights of small land owners in remote sections of this nation were protected. What was the urgency, Madam Speaker? Why could it not have said to us then that it needed one or two hours of House business to put through this simple protective measure? We are responsible people on this side of the House. We would have agreed. We would have agreed to take up two hours of our time to put through that important piece of legislation. The reality is that these Liberals were in such a rush to give away our gas they did not have even the slightest second thoughts about trampling on the civil liberties of a few land owners in southeastern British Columbia. What about the Tories? These Tories are really an incredible bunch. Just recently they have run ads in newspapers in my riding telling my constituents that I am against property rights and that they should all support the Conservatives if they want to keep their homes.
Let the record show who was fighting for the property rights of my constituents last fall when the Liberals sent in the riot squad police to take away the small property in my part of the riding. It certainly was not the Tories. I got up in the House and practically begged some of them to take part in the discussions but they were mysteriously quiet. I warned them that if the government got away with this on the B.C. section of the pipeline, it would not be long before it was expropriating land in Alberta. What was the response of the freedom fighters to my right? It was total, absolute silence. It seems they were more concerned with the property rights of Bob Blair and the Foothills Pipe Lines company than with the property rights of a couple of small land owners in British Columbia. Let them put that in their newspaper advertisements.
In any event, the deed was done. The government, which has absolutely no shame, allowed the police to occupy the lands of my constituents and then told them they had absolutely no legal remedies. This was taking place in November, at the
March 6, 1981

same time as the Liberals, in the constitutional committee, were trying to persuade us that they were the champions of civil liberties.
In the House I was forced to direct my questions to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) since there was no way I could question the real culprit, Senator Olson. With no disrespect intended to the minister, he clearly did not know anything about the situation and consistently provided me with contradictory, ill-informed answers. As for Senator Olson, he generally refused to answer my phone calls, preferring to have me deal with his assistants. I will never forget being told by one of the senator's assistants that there was no problem in my riding because even though the police had occupied the constituents' property, none of the local people had responded by shooting back! He was clearly proud that the government had managed to avoid getting itself into a military situation with my constituents.
By now the situation in Yahk has calmed down somewhat. The people are relieved that they are finally getting this bill, but are very frustrated and hurt since it is difficult for them to bargain effectively when their land has already been occupied and the pipeline is already in place.
There is, however, one specific concern we still have and I should like to relate it quickly. I believe there should be a provision in the bill which sets down very clearly the width of the right-of-way. It should be defined very clearly in the bill and not fought out through negotiation, mediation or arbitration. But there is nothing in the bill on this matter, and I am sorry about that.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I should like to urge the House to give speedy passage to this bill. My only regret is that the government did not find the time to do this last July. That would have meant a great deal of needless suffering would not have taken place in Kootenay East-Revelstoke.
Finally, I should like to congratulate the four Yahk residents who fought the bulk of this battle. Against the forces of armed riot police, heartless bureaucrats and fancy corporate lawyers, these four men fought until they got what they deserved, Bill C-60. We should take off our hats to these residents of Yahk, British Columbia.
Before I close my remarks, on behalf of these four residents of Yahk, British Columbia, I should like to present the minister with a shirt from Yahk, British Columbia, so that he will longer remember the residents of Yahk.

speakeroldname: Mr. Doug Anguish (The Battlefords-Meadow Lake) moved:
subsubtopic: AMENDMENT ALLOWING MORTGAGE REDUCTION THROUGH USE OF RRSP
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should consider the advisability of amending the Income Tax Act to provide that a taxpayer may, as an acceptable investment under the provisions relating to Registered Retirement Savings Plans, reduce the mortgage on the taxpayer's principal residence by paying a lump sum from a self-administered Registered Retirement Savings Plan.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I recognize that only a small percentage of Canadians take advantage of Registered Retirement Savings Plans, but if the government is going to continue with RRSPs, I would like the government to consider the resolution about which I will speak today. I ask hon. members not to talk it out but instead to allow the resolution to go through so that the government can consider the advisability of allowing homeowners to make a large payment annually toward their mortgages and have the payment credited toward a self-administered retirement savings plan.
I will not talk at length; I think the resolution is selfexplanatory. However, I want to mention the main advantages of the resolution in the event the government is willing to accept it.
First, there is immediate tax relief in the taxation year to families who are fortunate enough to own their own homes, just as has applied to RRSPs in the past. Second, people who have homes with mortgages held by banks or credit unions would own their homes and have clear title to those homes in a much shorter period of time. For example, if people took full advantage of such a program, they would be able to own their homes outright within about ten years as opposed to the usual 25-year amortization period. The third benefit applicable to this resolution, if it were to go through, is that people would be paying substantially less interest to mortgage companies, which in turn would allow a fourth benefit. This fourth benefit would allow people a larger discretionary income much sooner in their lives than otherwise. It would give them an increased discretionary income and, instead of paying toward a home, which is usually the largest investment the average Canadian makes, that money could be invested in the Canadian economy. That would be a step forward in helping Canadians gain more solid control of their own economy because home owners would be able to invest in Canada's economy after their largest single investment of a home is paid off.
I ask members not to talk out this resolution. I hope the government will seriously consider including individual's own
mortgages as part of the self-administered retirement savings plans.

speakeroldname: Mr. John Evans (Parliamentary Secretary to Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: AMENDMENT ALLOWING MORTGAGE REDUCTION THROUGH USE OF RRSP
speechtext:
On the surface, this proposal might appear both uncomplicated and quite attractive. As the hon. member for The Battlefords-Meadow Lake (Mr. Anguish) has indicated, it would allow a taxpayer to reduce the mortgage on his or her home by means of a lump sum payment out of self-administered registered retirement savings plan. In a period of high interest rates, such as we are experiencing now, this has a particular plausible and appealing look to it.
If we examine the idea more closely, however, it becomes apparent that the result would be to confer a very considerable financial benefit on a particular group of taxpayers, and, as 1 will show at the end of my comments, it would provide for a very substantial potential loophole in the tax system. In fact, to use the registered retirement savings plan in a fashion described by the hon. member for The Battlefords-Meadow Lake would tend to override the basic rationale of the RRSP system.
The purpose of a registered retirement savings plan system is to provide a tax deferral to allow people to save money to provide for their retirement years. Within quite generous ceilings, taxpayers can avoid current income taxation on these savings, in effect the RRSP permits a deferral of taxation until the time the savings are withdrawn from that plan at the time of retirement or at some earlier date. If this occurs during the taxpayer's retirement years, it is likely that his or her tax rate is lower than it was during the working years, and this benefit is added to the considerable advantage of the long-term tax deferral conferred by the RRSP.
This proposal would change the tax deferral notion of the registered retirement savings plan to a tax exemption.
1 will explain that briefly. For example, if an individual were to have a self-administered registered retirement savings plan of some considerable sum, he would be allowed, under this particular proposal, to purchase a house, put a mortgage on it and then withdraw the funds from the registered retirement savings plan, pay off the house and then subsequently sell it. Since there is no capital gains tax on a principal residence he would be able to avoid tax completely by that particular method. As a result, it would provide a rather substantial tax loophole, primarily to those people who have houses and who have during their life time made enough income to be able to accumulate a substantial registered retirement savings plan.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT ALLOWING MORTGAGE REDUCTION THROUGH USE OF RRSP
speechtext: Try putting safeguards in to prevent that.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: AMENDMENT ALLOWING MORTGAGE REDUCTION THROUGH USE OF RRSP
speechtext:
These are not the people about whom the hon. member for The Battlefords-Meadow Lake is really concerned. He would be opening up a tax loophole, and, as a member of the New Democratic Party, he would soon be wishing he could find some way to close it.
Registered retirement savings plans are of particular usefulness to self-employed Canadians who do not have the
March 6, 1981

benefit of an employer sponsored pension plan. They are also valuable to others who want to supplement an employer pension plan.
The financial attractiveness of RRSPs is obvious to anyone who has noticed the recent high-powered advertising campaigns of financial firms intended to attract RRSP investments before the March 2 deadline for 1980 contributions. Their value is also obvious in looking at recent Department of Finance studies of the value of federal tax expenditures. Tax expenditures are the various special incentives and benefits which our tax system provides. It is estimated that by 1980, the cumulative total, the total of all tax expenditures or savings which have been conferred through these plans since their inception to the current date in 1980, would be $22 billion in tax deferrals and reductions provided through the deductibility of payments into RRSPs and into registered pension plans. Most of this is accounted for by registered pension plans which would not be affected by the proposal put forward by the hon. member this afternoon, because these registered retirement savings plans are more widespread and have been in place for a longer period of time.
But it is estimated that $4.6 billion of the $22 billion total is attributable to tax deferrals under registered retirement savings plans. With such a valuable tax concession provided by RRSPs, it is only good sense to make sure that this benefit is not abused. One of the most essential safeguards is to ensure that these tax exempt or tax deferred savings do remain in the form of investments rather than being used for current consumption prior to retirement.
For example, consider what would happen under existing rules if a lump sum payment were made from a self-administered RRSP to reduce the taxpayer's home mortgage. If the RRSP did not acquire an interest in the mortgage or the property, the RRSP would be deregistered and the full amount of funds in the plan would be included in the taxpayer's income at that time. If the RRSP did, by some means, acquire an interest in the mortgage or property, the value of that interest would be included in the taxpayer's income at that time. Under both conditions with the existing rules, that would place the entire amount removed from the RRSP into current income. It would be fully taxable at that time at the marginal tax rate of the individual concerned.
These are strict rules, but they reflect the importance of protecting the treasury against abuse of the valuable tax advantage conferred by RRSPs.
Consider what the proposal in this motion would do. It would permit a taxpayer, in effect, to pay for part of the cost of his home and to deduct the amount from his income subject to tax. He could eventually pay off his mortgage and use tax exempt earnings to do it. I suggest this would be giving him a really inordinate advantage, and at the expense of the rest of Canadian taxpayers.
This motion would therefore confer a very preferred tax advantage on a particular group of taxpayers-those having a
Mortgages
home with a mortgage on it, and running a self-administered registered retirement savings plan.
We should remind ourselves that not every Canadian taxpayer has a large enough income that he has a surplus available for investment in an RRSP. Among those who do invest in RRSPs, not everyone has the financial ability-or can afford the expert advice-to administer his own RRSP. We have to remember that this proposal applies only to self-administered RRSPs and not those administered by a trust company or some other financial institution. Certainly not every Canadian owns his own home or indeed wishes to.
There does exist one tax measure by which a person can use tax exempt savings to purchase a home. This is the registered home ownership savings plan. It is designed to assist the home buying plans of people who do not now own their home and never have in the past. There is an annual limit of $1,000 in the amount of tax exempt savings that can be put into a RHOSP. The proposal before us today has no such limitation.
If we are asked to provide this proposed tax advantage for home owners we should look at the existing major tax advantages for home owners. Let me refer again to the finance department study of the value of tax expenditure provisions in the present tax laws. Tax deductibility of payments into registered home ownership savings plans was worth an estimated $95 million last year. When capital gains taxation was introduced with tax reform, an exception was made for capital gains on a taxpayer's principal residence. This would lead to the anomaly or tax loophole that I mentioned earlier in my remarks.
I do not dispute this decision, but we should be aware of the value of the exemption from tax on this sort of capital gain: the tax expenditure study estimates it at $3.5 billion for 1980 alone. The same study finds that the non-taxation of the imputed income from the equity of home owners in their own residences was worth an estimated $5 billion last year. It can be argued that this amounts to non-taxation of a hypothetical value.
It is a fact, however, that people who invest in their own home do so in the general recognition that there is a very real benefit in the fact that this particular investment is not subject to taxation. They know that, in contrast, they would have to pay for renting their home with after tax dollars. So it is beyond dispute that our existing tax system provides very strong support toward home ownership, much stronger support than is often realized.
It may be argued that people who owe on mortgages are having a difficult time during this period of high interest rates. But that is a problem which faces many others besides homeowners. Among home owners, it is a problem mainly for those who have to renew their mortgages at increased interest rates that currently prevail. I do not think we should seek a solution to the problem of high interest rates in a measure which benefits only home owners, including home owners who do not have to renew their mortgages under current conditions, but which does nothing for other Canadians in financial difficulties as the result of these interest rates.

March 6, 1981
Mortgages
The proposal in this motion would discriminate on another count as well. An RRSP is primarily intended to provide retirement income for those who are not covered by industrial pension plans or inadequately covered by such plans. Members of these other pension plans cannot use their plans to pay off their home mortgages, and it would be quite unfair to these people if we allowed RRSPs to be used to reduce mortgage debt and further restricted it to RRSPs that have to be self-administered.
The official opposition, when they formed the government attempted to legislate a tax credit plan to offset mortgage and property tax payments. This party opposed that measure as a highly discriminatory plan, and an economically unwise one as well. The December 1979 budget of the former minister of finance estimated its cost would have been over $1.2 billion for the coming 1981-82 fiscal year, rising to more than $2.8 billion in 1983-84.
The New Democratic Party at that time opposed the mortgage and property tax credit plan of the former Conservative government, primarily because of its discriminatory nature. 1 suggest to the hon. member for The Battlefords-Meadow Lake that his proposal embodies the same kind of discrimination.
Finally, I have not attempted to estimate its cost in forgone revenues to the federal treasury, but 1 have no doubt it would be substantial. At a time when we are trying to work toward a steady reduction of the federal deficit, the proposal today can only be considered to be a serious mistake.
Mir. Rene Cousineau (Gatineau): Mr. Speaker, it is difficult to see how one can support this motion, either on grounds of equity or economics. On the face of it, the proposal has a nice ring to it-we let home owners retire their mortgages by using their RRSP savings. But if we look closely at how it is done, the approach discriminates, favouring only one segment of the population that would be in a position to take advantage of it. Besides that, we would be creating another new tax expenditure, one which could add substantially to the budgetary deficit without really accomplishing any economic purpose.
There is a certain atmosphere of deja vu in this discussion. The hon. member for The Battlefords-Meadow Lake (Mr. Anguish) is proposing a tax advantage to home owners, though not as generous as the tax credit for mortgage interest and property taxes presented in 1979 by the former Conservative government. But it still discriminates, through its total exclusion of taxpayers who rent their homes. I am reminded of the declaration by the hon. member for Broadview-Greenwood (Mr. Rae) in that 1979 debate:
We are not prepared to support a policy which gives to one group at the expense of another.
That is recorded in Hansard at page 1504 of November 20, 1979. Although today's proposal would not give quite as open-handedly, the principle is the same. I do not think my hon. colleague had the honour of being in this House at that time three weeks before "D-night", or defeat night, but this
gave him a chance to be elected on February 18 and to express his views. I congratulate him on that.
On the face of it, it might appear that permitting a taxpayer to make lump sum payments against his mortgage from a self-administered RRSP is simply allowing him to use his own savings in the way he wants. However, those savings have accumulated in the RRSP exempt from taxation when they were earned, and the investment income of the RRSP was equally tax exempt.
Huge amounts of income tax revenue which would otherwise have been paid to the treasury have in many cases been deferred for many years, until the taxpayer retires. This has been done to assist taxpayers to save for their retirement years. There would be no justification for the government's forgoing income tax on earnings which are then spent on current consumption, yet that is what is proposed by this motion.
The motion discriminates. As I have noted, in that it excludes Canadians who rent their homes. If a person owned his home clear of any mortgage, he could not benefit from this proposal. To take advantage of the motion he must first of all be able to save enough to buy a home, mortgage it and then he must be able to save enough additional money to make lump sum reductions in the capital amount owing on his mortgage. Unfortunately, not all Canadians are in that position. Finally, he must have the financial skills to set up a self-administered RRSP or, more likely, pay for the advice of a professional consultant to do it. I think we must conclude that this measure would not have a very wide application among Canadian taxpayers.
There is another way in which this measure would discriminate among Canadians. It would allow holders of self-administered RRSPs to use these retirement savings for mortgage reduction. But what of all the other Canadians who have chosen to save for retirement in other ways, through insurance company contracts, for example, or, more likely, through industrial pension plans where they work? These savings, like RRSPs, have benefited from deferral of income tax on earnings put into these retirement plans. They would not be allowed, under this motion, to withdraw their savings for the purpose of reducing mortgage debt.
We must admit that the Income Tax Act does contain provisions which give special, favourable tax treatment to particular groups or favour certain types of activities. That is one of the things which makes the tax law so complex. These special provisions are justified on the ground that they promote certain economic activities which are generally beneficial to society.
Are there similar economic justifications for the proposal before us? Does it, for example, encourage home ownership? I suggest not really, since in order to benefit the taxpayer would have to be a home owner already. We already have the registered home ownership savings plan which encourages taxpayers to buy their own homes. It cannot be said that this proposal promotes savings, since it would not apply until after the savings had already been accumulated under the incentive of the RRSP tax deferral.
March 6, 1981

To some extent this proposal would be helpful in this period of high interest rates for home owners who are refinancing their mortgages, but it would also benefit those who do not have to refinance mortgages and have the benefit of mortgage contracts at lower interest rates. It would amount to a subsidy for certain Canadians, and that is the important part of my argument, against the pressures of high interest rates, but it would do nothing for the majority of citizens and, of course, it would be treating only the symptom and not the cause of high interest rates. 1 do not think there is an economic justification for the discrimination this motion would create.
1 honestly think it would be a serious mistake to adopt a measure such as this, which would undermine the basic purpose of RRSP savings for retirement and create a huge loophole in that tax incentive system while achieving no lasting economic advantage for society.

Mr. Speaker, 1 should like to say just a few words. After all, there still are 15 minutes before this 40-minute hour comes to an end.
i have listened with interest to the criticisms put forward by the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Evans) and by the hon. member for Gatineau (Mr. Cousineau) with respect to the resolution before us as moved by my colleague, the hon. member for The Battlefords-Meadow Lake (Mr. Anguish). I would be less than honest if I did not admit that some of their criticisms are valid and certainly have to be considered. 1 would have felt happier about their speeches, however, if they had found it possible to see that there might be something good in this resolution and if, instead of damning it completely, they had made suggestions as to how it might have been limited so as to achieve the purpose I believe my colleague has in mind. I have not discussed it with him and, if I speak for him and say what I should not, I trust he will correct me.
However, I think what he has in mind is that there are older people approaching retirement who have some money in RRSPs and feel it would improve their retirement situation if they could get rid of the mortgages on their family homes, even at the expense of having a little less pension income than that which they could have had from their RRSPs. I would like to see that part of it studied.
My hon. friend, the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance, admits there is a parallel between RRSPs and RHOSPs. He points out that RHOSPs are mostly for young families seeking to purchase their first homes. They are of no help to people of 60 or 63 years of age or more who are approaching retirement but are still carrying mortgages. Even if it was narrowed to that area and even if restrictions were placed so that it could not be used for speculative purposes or for getting cheap money to invest somewhere else, I think my friend, the hon. member for The Battlefords-Meadow Lake, has a point, and I would like to see it looked at more favourably. I would like to see it looked at as something to study rather than something just to reject out of hand.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT ALLOWING MORTGAGE REDUCTION THROUGH USE OF RRSP
speechtext:
I have done a lot of head scratching and tried to think of some method by which we might be able to reduce that burden and yet be fair to all the taxpayers of Canada. I happen to be one of those who is saddled with a mortgage. 1 suppose I should not use the term "saddled" because no one forced me to take a mortgage either on my home in Ottawa or on my home in New Brunswick. 1 did so of my own free will. I mortgaged my future. I suppose that is what life is all about, so I am not complaining about it. But it does make it binding sometimes to have a large mortgage, particularly if you are paying high rates of interest.
In considering this motion today, one is reminded of another occasion on which a proposal was put to the House to provide a tax advantage to home owners. That was in 1979 when the former Conservative government attempted to legislate a personal income tax credit to help reduce the burden of mortgage payments and of local property taxes.
1 had a number of problems with the proposal. The first was that it provided the greatest advantage to people who could afford the largest mortgages. Second, 1 found it difficult to understand why the federal government should be called upon to subsidize the burden of property taxes. It seems to me if there is to be an alleviation of property taxes, many of the provincial governments in this country would want to take a look at what was done in New Brunswick in the mid-1960s with the program of equal opportunity when the property tax assessment was equalized across the province and the rate of property taxation was equalized as well. The rate was based upon the so-called actual market value of your property.
One rate was established for individual residences and another rate was established for business residences, income properties, and those rates were the same all across the province. The individual municipalities could add an additional levy to pay for municipal services, but that levy was paid also on the provincial assessment level applied to all residences and all business properties across the province. As a result, instead of residential property taxation increasing in New Brunswick in the last 15 years, in many cases it has actually decreased. That is particularly true for the provincial portion of residential property taxation. Out of that levy, the basic costs of

March 6, 1981
Mortgages
education, health care and justice is paid by the province so that there is a uniform system of these services.
One of the reasons property taxes are so high in some municipalities compared to others in other provinces of Canada is that the provincial governments in many cases have not taken the initiative to impose a fair system of assessment on properties and have not taken over the responsibility for basic educational, medical, and hospitalization costs and costs of the administration of justice across the province.
The hon. member for The Battlefords-Meadow Lake (Mr. Anguish) was not a Member of Parliament when the Tories brought in their ill-fated mortgage deductibility scheme, but he should be aware that members of his own party at that time supported the Liberal party in opposing that bill because of the inequities in it. Both parties saw the bill as unfairly giving special treatment to home owners while ignoring tenants, and giving the largest tax breaks to those who needed them least.
It is a little surprising that the hon. member proposes this resolution which, at first glance at least, looks to be much the same. It suggests that somebody who has a self-administered Registered Retirement Savings Plan can take a lump sum out of it, apply it to his mortgage and still escape income tax on that money. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre suggested that people approaching their retirement age who had a substantial amount of money in a Registered Retirement Savings Plan might find it to their advantage to put that money on their mortgage rather than to leave it in the Registered Retirement Savings Plan. This is not the reason Registered Retirement Savings Plans were established.
The number of self-administered registered savings plans is small, proportional to all Registered Retirement Savings Plans in the nation. Therefore, if this motion were adopted, we would be creating a piece of tax legislation which would be very, very discriminatory in its application. If we followed the logic of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, we would have the anomaly where the elderly person who took money out of his plan to apply against his mortgage would find out a few years later when he retired that he must sell his house in order to have a retirement income. So, I cannot really see the benefit.
The registered retirement savings plan system is essentially a plan of tax deferral for people who now have sufficient earnings to put aside some money, without paying tax on the principal, in order to build up a retirement fund. It is not possible for everyone to do that. For many people, all their earnings must go to providing shelter, education for their families, clothing, medical care and the various things which are necessary to rear a family. Many people in family situations who pay taxes cannot afford retirement savings plans. Therefore, they would have to pay income tax to subsidize the people who have been granted tax exemptions on the money they have put into their registered retirement savings plans. If we agreed to this motion, they could take out their money, apply it to their mortgage and still receive the tax exemption. Then those who cannot afford retirement savings plans and perhaps are just making ends meet by paying their own mortgages are required to subsidize the people who are making lump sum payments on their mortgages. That is not a very equitable proposition.
It is clear that valuable tax advantages are provided through the RRSP system. In fact, it is estimated that in the relatively brief period this plan has been in existence, over $4.5 billion in tax deferrals have accumulated up to 1980. That is why the tax law is careful to ensure that if any withdrawals are made from these funds for purposes other than retirement the tax deferral is terminated immediately. I believe that is as it should be. If we give a tax deferral for a specific reason, then it should apply only to that reason. If we start making exemptions to the rule, where will it end? Next week there will be another motion so that it can apply, for example, to an educational fund or to the tuition fees of one's son or daughter. It would go on and on, until there was a pot-pourri over which there would be no control.
In my opinion, the motion goes against the very principle of RRSPs when it proposes that a taxpayer be allowed to reduce the mortgage on his home by these lump sum payments.
